ds: Recruitment, transport or harbouring of people by force, fraud or coercion for exploitation, including sexual exploitation, labour exploitation and domestic servitude. Financial footprints include accounts controlled by third parties, payments for advertising, accommodation and travel, and cash proceeds moved through money mules. Indicators are signals for victim-centred escalation, not proof.

src.t: FATF and APG, Financial Flows from Human Trafficking (2018)
FATF, Money Laundering Risks Arising from Trafficking in Human Beings and Smuggling of Migrants (2011)
UNODC, Global Report on Trafficking in Persons (biennial; specify edition e.g. 2024)
Egmont Group, public material on financial intelligence and human trafficking

cn.rt: Third-party controlled accounts, cash deposits, adverts and travel/accommodation spend, plus coerced credit.

rat: Controlled accounts, cash deposits, adverts and short-stay bookings; front businesses (e.g. massage, car-wash, restaurant) with poor payroll evidence.

ind.n: Account controlled by a third party
ind.cx: Someone other than the account holder appears to hold the card, PIN or online credentials, accompanying the holder or accessing from a shared device.
ind.fp: Family members, carers and partners may legitimately help with banking.
ind.ds: Signs that a third party holds the card, PIN, credentials or device, or that funds and activity belong to someone other than the named holder.
ind.cn: Account controlled or used by someone other than the holder

ind.n: Multiple unrelated accounts opened with the same address or phone
ind.cx: Several new customers share contact details, often in accommodation used to house workers.
ind.fp: Shared households, student housing and hostels create shared addresses.
ind.ds: Unrelated customers or applicants share the same phone, email, address, device or bank account, including mail drops and shared accommodation.
ind.cn: Multiple customers sharing contact details or addresses

ind.n: Payments for online adverts and hotels or short-stay lets for multiple rooms
ind.cx: Frequent purchases of escort or commercial sex adverts, bulk hotel bookings and short-term rentals paid by the same card or account.
ind.fp: Hospitality and legitimate escort or event businesses exist.
ind.ds: Frequent purchases of escort or commercial sex adverts, bulk hotel bookings and short-term rentals paid by the same card or account.

ind.n: Cash deposits followed by quick transfers to a handler in another city
ind.cx: Multiple low-value cash deposits by different people into one account, then rapid onward transfer or ATM withdrawal.
ind.fp: Group business or family collections can resemble this.
ind.ds: Cash deposited is quickly withdrawn or transferred onward, including to another location or to unhosted wallets.
ind.cn: Rapid onward movement after cash credits

ind.n: Wage or benefit payments immediately withdrawn by another person
ind.cx: Salary, welfare or loan proceeds are withdrawn in full by someone not the account holder or sent to a third party on receipt.
ind.fp: Remittance to family is common after payday.
ind.ds: Salary, welfare or loan proceeds are withdrawn in full by someone not the account holder or sent to a third party on receipt.

ind.n: Customer appears fearful, unable to speak freely, or lacks own ID
ind.cx: Customer accompanied by a person who speaks for them, avoids eye contact, lacks access to documents or appears coached.
ind.fp: Language barriers and shyness have other explanations.
ind.ds: Another person speaks for, accompanies or dictates instructions to the customer, who may appear fearful, scripted or unable to explain the activity.
ind.cn: Customer accompanied, directed or coached by a third party

ind.n: Travel and visa fee payments for groups from the same recruiter
ind.cx: Bulk payments for flights, visas and recruitment fees to a labour recruiter, sometimes debt-financed.
ind.fp: Genuine recruitment agencies charge fees in some corridors.
ind.ds: Bulk payments for flights, visas and recruitment fees to a labour recruiter, sometimes debt-financed.

ind.n: Business front for exploitation with revenue not matching staff
ind.cx: Massage, nail, car-wash, restaurant or agricultural entity with cash patterns and many resident staff but poor payroll evidence.
ind.fp: Small businesses in these sectors are overwhelmingly legitimate.
ind.ds: Reported revenue, payroll or resident staff do not match the typical costs and workforce of the stated business model.
ind.cn: Business revenue inconsistent with staffing or operating costs

ind.n: Adverse media or intelligence on trafficking network associations
ind.cx: Customer or counterparties named in credible reports or law enforcement requests relating to trafficking.
ind.ds: Counterparties, suppliers, respondents or controllers appear in adverse media, law-enforcement notices or intelligence connected to financial crime, abuse, forced labour or organised crime.
ind.cn: Adverse media or intelligence linking counterparties to criminal activity

ctl.ds: Fingerprints devices, IP addresses, emulators and network attributes to link applications, sessions and accounts and to flag shared or anomalous infrastructure. It exposes mule rings and multiple-account abuse.

Trains branch, contact-centre and relationship staff to ask open questions, recognise coaching, coercion, pressure and evasion and escalate with authority to pause. It strengthens the human control at the point of contact.

Provides discreet escalation routes and private conversation procedures so staff can refer suspected victims of exploitation, coercion or trafficking to specialists, police and support organisations. It prioritises victim safety.
Clusters customers, vendors and entities that share addresses, phones, devices, officers or bank details, including against staff records. It reveals common control and hidden relationships.

Translates published and sanitised typologies and red flags into targeted monitoring scenarios and context-aware rules that are reviewed periodically. It aligns monitoring with known criminal methods.

ctl.n: Fan-in, fan-out and funnel account detection
ctl.ds: Detects accounts receiving from many unrelated senders, or sending to many beneficiaries, followed by consolidation or onward movement. It surfaces collector, funnel and mule structures.
Alerts when inflows are quickly moved out with little retained balance, including cash-in fast-out and rapid conversion or cash-out. It reveals accounts used as conduits for layering.

Briefs front-line, onboarding and investigation staff on current red flags, typologies and escalation routes, including sector-specific patterns and professional-enabler behaviours. It improves recognition of suspicious activity that rules alone cannot see.

ctl.n: Labour provider and recruiter due diligence
ctl.ds: Verifies licences, ownership, registration, tax compliance and wage-payment evidence of labour providers and recruiters at onboarding and review, and checks recruitment practices. It reduces exposure to exploitative labour supply and undeclared work.

ctl.n: Payroll and worker payment flow analytics
ctl.ds: Compares payroll flows with declared headcount, checks that wages reach workers' own accounts and flags cash payroll, recruiter payments and many-to-one wage patterns. It surfaces undeclared work and labour exploitation.

ctl.n: Purpose and intended nature of relationship
ctl.ds: Captures and challenges the stated purpose of the account, expected activity, volumes and geographies at onboarding, creating a baseline against which later behaviour is judged. Vague or implausible answers prompt further enquiry or decline.

Runs continuous screening of customers, owners, introducers, suppliers and counterparties against curated news, leaks, regulatory notices and enforcement releases, with reliability grading and identity disambiguation. It surfaces negative information that registers and lists do not carry.
Participates in sector, regulator and public-private forums and platform cooperation to receive and share typologies and indicators where lawful. It keeps scenarios current.
